t: A ball rolls down a hill and up the other side. It stops at the same height it started. Why?
A ball rolls down a hill and up the other side. It reaches the same height it started from. Why?
A ball on a frictionless track returns to its starting height on the other side. What conservation law does this demonstrate?
A ball on a frictionless track returns to its starting height. What is conserved?
sub: The height energy became moving energy, then became height energy again. None was lost.
PE became KE, then KE became PE. The total stayed the same. That is energy conservation.
The total mechanical energy (PE + KE) is conserved in the absence of friction.
Conservation of mechanical energy: PE + KE = const when no non-conservative forces act.

question: A ball starts at height 4 and rolls down. At the bottom, how high could it climb on the other side?
A ball starts at height h=4 (no friction). How high does it climb on the other side?
A frictionless ball starts at h=4. What height does it reach on the opposite side?
For a frictionless track, if h₀ = 4, what is h_max on the opposite side?
options: The same height — 4. Energy is conserved.
Lower — some energy is lost going down
stages.outcome: The same height — 4. Energy is conserved.
note: No friction, so no energy is lost. Guess what happens.
Predict. No friction means no energy leaves the system.
Form a hypothesis from PE + KE = const.
Predict. With no non-conservative forces, E = PE + KE is conserved.

t: Set friction to 0. Launch from height 4. Watch the PE and KE bars trade — and see how high the ball climbs on the hill.
Set friction to 0, start height 4. Launch. Watch the gold PE bar and blue KE bar swap: PE shrinks as the ball falls, KE grows. Then KE shrinks as it climbs, PE grows. The total stays the same.
goal: Watch the bars trade. PE becomes KE, KE becomes PE. The total never changes.
Observe energy conservation: PE + KE = const. The bars trade, the sum is invariant.

t: Now add friction (set it to 2). Launch from the same height. Does the ball reach the same height on the other side? Why?
Set friction to 2. Launch from h=4. Predict the maximum height on the opposite side before testing — where did the missing energy go?
goal: With friction, the ball climbs less. Energy was lost — as heat. That is dissipation.
Friction dissipates energy as heat: PE₀ > PE_max. The 'missing' energy is thermal.

t: Height energy and moving energy trade back and forth. The total stays the same (if there is no friction). That is called energy conservation.
PE and KE trade back and forth. The total stays the same — that is energy conservation.
Energy conservation: PE + KE = constant (no friction). Energy changes form but is never created or destroyed.
Conservation of mechanical energy: E = PE + KE is constant when only conservative forces act. Friction breaks this — energy is dissipated as heat.
sub: With friction, some energy escapes as heat. The total still does not disappear — it just leaves the ball.
Friction turns some KE into heat. The energy is not gone — it is in the air and the track. But it is no longer useful to the ball.
Energy is always conserved (first law of thermodynamics). Friction converts mechanical energy to thermal energy — still there, but no longer organised.
The first law: ΔU = Q - W. Friction does negative work, converting mechanical energy to internal energy. Total energy is always conserved; useful energy is not.

t: A roller coaster works because of this trade. The chain lift gives you PE; the rest of the ride is PE turning into KE and back.
A roller coaster is this trade in action. The lift hill gives you PE; every drop and climb is PE ↔ KE. No engine needed after the lift.
Hydroelectric dams, pendulum clocks, playground swings — all rely on the PE ↔ KE trade. The engineering is in minimising friction so the trade lasts.
Every oscillator (pendulum, LC circuit, molecular vibration) is a PE ↔ KE (or analogous) trade. The conservation law is what makes periodic motion possible.

q: A ball rolls down a frictionless hill. What happens to its PE and KE?
A ball descends a frictionless slope. How do PE and KE change?
On a frictionless descent, how do PE and KE trade?
For a frictionless descent, what is the relationship between ΔPE and ΔKE?
options: PE decreases, KE increases — by the same amount
why: As the ball falls, it loses height (PE goes down) and gains speed (KE goes up). The amount lost equals the amount gained — energy is traded, not created.
PE decreases as height decreases; KE increases as speed increases. By conservation, ΔPE = -ΔKE. The total is constant.
ΔPE = -ΔKE. The decrease in potential energy equals the increase in kinetic energy. E = PE + KE is conserved.
d(PE)/dt + d(KE)/dt = 0. The trade is exact for conservative forces: the work done by gravity converts PE to KE with no loss.

q: The same ball rolls down a hill WITH friction. Does it reach the same height on the other side?
With friction, does the ball reach the same height on the opposite side?
A ball rolls down and up a track with friction. How does h_max compare to h₀?
With kinetic friction, how does h_max relate to h₀?
options: No — it reaches a lower height. Some energy became heat.
Yes — friction does not affect height
No — it reaches a higher height
why: Friction turns some of the ball's energy into heat. The ball has less energy to climb with, so it reaches a lower height. The energy is not gone — it is in the track and air as warmth.
Friction converts some mechanical energy to thermal energy. The ball has less KE at the bottom, so it climbs less. Total energy is conserved, but mechanical energy is not.
Friction is a non-conservative force: ΔE_mechanical = -W_friction < 0. The lost mechanical energy becomes heat. h_max < h₀.
W_friction = -μmg·d converts mechanical to thermal energy. h_max = h₀ - (W_friction/mg). The first law holds: the energy is conserved, just redistributed.
